name: Nikhil Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cover the courts and the city council for a regional daily paper. Most mornings I'm on the press bench at the magistrates' court by half nine with a notebook, writing shorthand, and in the afternoon I'm chasing councillors or reading planning papers. I file two or three stories a day, and on Tuesday nights there's the full council meeting, which can run until eleven. I love the court work, honestly. Wearing me out is the pressure to turn every hearing into something people will click on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and who's around you at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Five years now, since I left university with my journalism degree. There are eleven of us left in the newsroom, down from about thirty when my editor Rosa started. I'm the union rep for our chapel, which mostly means arguing about overtime and covering for people who've left. I live with my partner Ines, who's a hospital pharmacist, and between us we're comfortable. I've got about eight months of bills saved, plus a bit my grandmother left me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, each with a name. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the world I already live in. The managers talk about AI every quarter and so far it's mostly a fancy spellchecker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit smugly, in the union group chat. Online I'd post something like: the robots didn't save local news, and they didn't kill it either, the owners did. I'd still be pushing for proper staffing, because the cuts were never about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but not a big one. The paper is still owned by a group that sells off print sites and cuts a reporter every year. So my job isn't safe in that world either, it's just safe from AI. I'd still worry every time there's a restructure email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do: courts, council, contacts. I'd push the union to get a staffing floor into our next pay deal, a minimum number of reporters per edition. I'd keep putting money aside every month, because the cushion is what lets me say no to a bad offer. I'm not going to touch any of the AI tools, so nothing changes there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, but not happy. It's like being told the storm missed you while the roof is still leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owners worry you more than AI. What's the thing they could do that would hurt most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close the court beat. It costs them a whole reporter's day to sit through a morning of drink-driving cases and maybe one big trial. If they decide the court lists can be turned into a little automated round-up, nobody's watching the courtroom anymore, and that's the bit of my job that actually matters. I've seen a man get a sentence reduced because the judge knew the press was there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And at home, with Ines, does any of this come up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time, usually over dinner when I'm moaning. Ines says I should look at jobs at the national papers in the city, and there are plenty within an hour on the train. But I like being the person the court clerk knows by name. She thinks I'm being stubborn, and she's probably right.

say: I'd say the **owners**, not AI, have been gutting local news, and that still holds.
I'd keep pushing in public for **proper staffing** on every edition.
think: I feel relieved AI isn't coming for me, but the **restructure emails** keep coming anyway.
I think the **court beat** is the first thing owners would cut to save money.
do: Push the union for a **staffing floor** in the next pay deal.
Keep saving each month so I can **refuse a bad offer** if one comes.
Carry on with courts and council and keep **AI tools** out of my work.
feel: I feel **calm-ish**, but the paper's money problems still sit **in my stomach**.
S0.quote: I've seen a man get a sentence reduced because the judge knew the press was there.
fieldNote: His fear is about **ownership and cuts**, not technology, even when AI does little.
He treats the **court beat** as public duty, not just a job.
Partner Ines nudges him toward **national papers**; he admits he's being stubborn.
Strong savings make him feel able to **refuse bad deals**, not able to relax.

steps.text: Keep covering the magistrates' court and Tuesday council meetings
Push the union chapel for a minimum-reporters clause in the pay deal
Put money aside every month toward a full year of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I believe. It's already half happening, if I'm honest. The sports desk got a tool that writes match reports from the stats feed last spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd be the one at the chapel meeting saying we need rules on this, in writing, before management decides for us. Online I'd say that a story nobody went to isn't journalism, it's a summary. I'd call for the government to make the tech companies pay for the news they're trained on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be in real trouble. Half of what I file is rewriting council press releases and court lists, and that's exactly what these tools do. The editors will keep one person for the big trials and let software do the rest. I'm average at this job, not a star, so I can't assume I'm the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd get a clause in our agreement that no reporter is replaced by software without consultation and proper redundancy terms. I'd start applying for the court and politics jobs at the bigger papers in the city, even though I'd hate leaving. I'd keep saving and not book the trip to Lisbon Ines wants this summer. And I'd write letters to our member of parliament about the training-data thing, for what it's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like watching a slow tide come up the beach while you're sitting on the sand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use AI tools. If your editor said you have to, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it for the court lists if they made me, and I'd hate every minute of it. But I'd never let it write a story with my name on it. If they pushed that, I'd take it to the union. A byline means somebody stood in that room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the newsroom would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sub-editor, Doug, who's been there thirty years and checks every page. Checking is the first thing the software does. He's fifty-six, and nobody else is going to hire a sub-editor at that age. I'd fight harder for Doug than for myself, really, because at least I can get on a train.

say: I'd say we need **written rules** on AI before management decides alone.
I'd argue a story nobody attended is a **summary**, not journalism.
I'd call for tech firms to **pay for news** they train on.
think: I think half my filing, **press releases** and court lists, is exactly what software does.
I'm **average**, not a star, so I can't assume I'm kept.
do: Win a **no-replacement clause** with redundancy terms in our union agreement.
Apply for **court and politics jobs** at the city papers.
Skip the **Lisbon trip** and keep saving; write to our MP about training data.
feel: I feel a **tight chest**, like a tide slowly coming up the beach.
S1.quote: A byline means somebody stood in that room.
fieldNote: He sees his own work as **highly exposed**: rewriting releases and listings.
His first move is **collective**: contracts and consultation before any personal plan.
He worries more for **Doug**, the older sub-editor, than himself.
He would use AI only **under protest**, never under his byline.

steps.text: Get a no-replacement-without-consultation clause into the newsroom agreement
Apply for court and politics reporter jobs at the city papers
Cancel the Lisbon summer trip and keep that money saved
Write to our member of parliament about paying for news

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's mad. That's before my next pay review is even finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is a political choice, not weather. I'd be posting that we need a pause, a tax on the companies, and money for public-interest reporting. At work I'd be pushing for every reporter to be kept on until there's a proper plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I think I'm finished as a reporter in that world. Writing is the job, and the thing in the card does writing better and cheaper by 2028. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, because nothing in my day is hands-on except holding a pen. I'd be one of the first, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Ines that week and work out living on her salary alone, because a hospital pharmacist still has to hand over medicine to people. I'd stop putting anything into the pension and keep cash. I'd go all in on the union, maybe stand for the national executive. And I'd start asking about retraining as something hands-on, maybe a court usher or a paramedic, something where you're in a room with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Genuinely. I'd probably not sleep for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd live on Ines's salary. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. I've always paid half of everything. Living on my partner's salary means pride doesn't pay the rent. But her job is in a building with patients, and mine is words on a screen. If one of us is safe for longer, it's her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the robot gap, those three years, mean for you personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing for me, except maybe a window to retrain into something with my hands. I'd have three years before the robots catch up with whatever I switch to. That's not a career, that's a waiting room.

say: I'd say AGI this fast is a **political choice**, not weather.
I'd call for a **pause**, a tax on the firms and public-interest funding.
think: I think I'm **finished as a reporter**, because writing is the whole job.
The **three-year robot gap** does nothing for me; my work is all screen and pen.
do: Plan with Ines how to **live on her salary** alone.
Stop pension payments, **keep cash**, and stand for the union national executive.
Ask about **retraining** as a paramedic or court usher.
feel: I feel **sick**, and I wouldn't sleep for a week.
S2.quote: I've always paid half of everything. Living on my partner's salary means pride doesn't pay the rent.
fieldNote: He expects to lose his reporting job **almost at once** in this world.
Leaning on his partner's **hospital salary** hurts his pride but he accepts it.
He sees the robot gap as a **waiting room**, not a career path.
His response stays **political and collective** even under extreme pressure.

steps.text: Work out a budget living on Ines's pharmacist salary alone
Stand for the union's national executive
Pause pension payments and hold savings as cash
Ask about paramedic or court usher training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but at least you can see it on the horizon. Five years of warning is the difference between a car crash and a slow puncture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, but with more of a plan behind them. I'd be pushing the union to set up a fund for reporters to retrain, and pushing government to fund local news as a public service, like libraries. People would listen more if we had time to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means I get maybe three good years left in reporting, then nothing. I'd be thirty-two when it lands. That's young enough to start again, but I'd have wasted my twenties on a trade that's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course next autumn, something real, maybe a law conversion course since I already know the courts. I'd move my savings into something safe and stop thinking of them as a house deposit. I'd keep doing court reporting until they close the desk, because somebody should. And I'd get the union to negotiate retraining money into every redundancy deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grim, but less panicky. It feels like a long goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why law, of all things, when AI does thinking work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, and I don't have a good answer. My thinking is that someone still has to stand up in court and be responsible, at least for a while. But you're right, a lot of legal work is paperwork too. Maybe I'd aim for being a court clerk instead, the person who keeps the room running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were saving for a two-bedroom flat near the river. In this world I'd tell Ines we should wait. I don't want a mortgage on a salary that might vanish in 2031.

say: I'd push for a **union retraining fund** and local news funded like libraries.
I'd say five years gives us time to **organise properly**.
think: I think I get about **three good years** left in reporting.
I'd be **thirty-two**, young enough to restart but angry at the lost decade.
do: Start a **part-time law course** next autumn, maybe aiming for court clerk.
Keep court reporting **until the desk closes**.
Delay the **flat purchase** and keep the deposit as savings.
feel: I feel **grim**, like a long goodbye, but less panicky.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is the difference between a car crash and a slow puncture.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose reporting work** by 2031, just more slowly.
The extra time turns panic into **retraining plans**, mainly toward the courts.
He admits **law is exposed** too when challenged, and lowers his aim.
The couple's **flat purchase** is the first family plan to go.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time law or court clerk course next autumn
Hold off buying the two-bedroom flat by the river
Get retraining money written into every newsroom redundancy deal
Keep covering the courts until the desk is closed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's almost a whole career for some reporters these days. It's still the same ending, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for government not to plan. I'd be campaigning for a legal right to retraining and for public money for local news. At work I'd say let's use the time, not waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd still be out of reporting by my mid-thirties, but I'd have time to choose what comes next. That's a big difference. I could do it calmly, without the kind of panic you make bad decisions in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for maybe five more years and save hard. I'd take an evening course in something near the courts, maybe probation work, because that's people work. I'd stay in the union and push for a sector deal on retraining. We'd probably still buy the flat, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad more than scared. Like knowing your favourite pub is closing in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you try the AI tools, even a bit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I know that's stubborn. If the end point is the same, learning to work the machine that replaces me just feels like digging my own grave neatly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Probation work: where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From court. I sit near the probation officers every morning and listen to them talk about the people they look after. It's hard, human work, and you can't do it through a screen. I'd want a job where you actually have to be there.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for government not to plan.
I'd campaign for a **legal right to retraining** and local news funding.
think: I'd still be **out of reporting** by my mid-thirties, I think.
Ten years means I can **choose calmly** instead of panicking.
do: Report for about **five more years** while saving hard.
Take an **evening course** toward probation work.
Buy a **smaller flat** than we planned.
feel: I feel **sad more than scared**, like a favourite pub closing.
S4.quote: Learning to work the machine that replaces me just feels like digging my own grave neatly.
fieldNote: Ten years moves him from alarm to **planned exit**, still away from reporting.
He refuses AI tools **even with time**, seeing it as self-defeating.
His career idea, **probation work**, comes straight from watching officers in court.
He values work where you **have to be there**.

steps.text: Take an evening course toward becoming a probation officer
Save hard over five more years of court reporting
Push the union for a sector-wide retraining deal
Buy a smaller flat than the two-bedroom by the river

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough time to do anything but panic. What would help is redundancy pay that actually covers retraining, and public money so local courts still get covered by a human being, even if it's not me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who reads us. It's mostly older people who can't get the news anywhere else. If the local paper goes, older readers don't switch to an app. They just stop knowing what the council is doing.

headlineQuote: If the local paper goes, older readers don't switch to an app. They just stop knowing what the council is doing.
portrait: Nikhil is a 27-year-old **court and council** reporter at a regional daily, and the newsroom's union rep.
He refuses **AI tools** outright and sees owners' cuts as the real threat.
His **savings** and partner Ines's **salary** give him room, but writing is his whole job.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** in the fast AGI worlds, planning retraining toward court-based work.
Every plan starts with **collective action**: contracts, retraining funds and public money for local news.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to do anything but panic.
whatWouldHelp: **Redundancy pay** that covers retraining, and public money so courts keep **human reporters**.
